title: C# in a nutshell
description: What kind of language C# is, how a C# program runs on .NET, and value versus reference types.

content.title: A language made for .NET
content.body:
C# (say "C sharp") is a general-purpose, object-oriented language created at Microsoft by Anders Hejlsberg and released in 2000. It is statically typed: the compiler knows the type of every value and rejects many mistakes before the program even runs.

C# code does not run by itself. The compiler (called Roslyn) turns it into Intermediate Language (IL), stored in an assembly: a .dll file. When the program starts, the .NET runtime (the CLR) compiles that IL into machine code just in time (JIT), and a garbage collector frees the memory of the objects nobody uses anymore.

Today's .NET is open source and runs on Windows, Linux and macOS.

content.question: You run dotnet build on a C# project. What does the compiler produce?

choices.text: Intermediate Language (IL) in an assembly, a .dll file
Machine code for your processor, and nothing else
JavaScript that runs in the browser
Java bytecode for the JVM

content.explanation: The C# compiler produces IL. The .NET runtime turns it into machine code while the program runs (JIT compilation). Compiling straight to machine code (Native AOT) is possible, but it is an option, not the default.

content.question: C# is statically typed. What does that mean?

choices.text: The compiler knows the type of every expression, so int n = "hello"; is rejected before the program runs
Every variable has to be declared with the static keyword
Types are only checked while the program runs
You always have to write the type: var is not allowed

content.explanation: Static typing means type errors are found at compile time. static is an unrelated keyword, and var is still statically typed: the compiler infers the type.

choices.text: It does not compile: var made total an int
total now contains the text "forty-two"
total now contains 42 again, the text is ignored
It compiles, but throws an exception when it runs

content.explanation: var does not mean "any type". The compiler infers int from 42, and total stays an int forever, so assigning a string is a compile error.

content.title: Value types and reference types
content.body:
Every C# type is either a value type or a reference type.

Value types (int, double, bool, char, enums and structs) hold their value directly. Copying the variable copies the value: the two copies are independent.

Reference types (classes, arrays, lists, string...) live on the heap; the variable only holds a reference to the object. Copying the variable copies the reference, so both variables point to the same object.

string is a reference type, but it is immutable: a method like ToUpper() returns a new string instead of changing the existing one.

choices.text: It does not compile

content.explanation: int is a value type: b = a copies the value 1 into b. Changing b afterwards does not touch a.

choices.text: It depends on the garbage collector

content.explanation: List<int> is a class, so a reference type: q = p copies the reference, and p and q are the same list. Adding through q is visible through p.

content.question: Who frees the memory of the objects your program no longer uses?

choices.text: The garbage collector of the .NET runtime, automatically
You, by calling delete on each object
The operating system, but only when the program ends
The compiler, which inserts free() calls at build time

content.explanation: The garbage collector finds objects that nothing references anymore and reclaims their memory. For resources like files or connections, you still call Dispose (often with using).

content.question: Which statements about .NET today are true?

choices.text: It runs on Windows, Linux and macOS
It is open source
It only runs on Windows
C# is the only language that runs on .NET

content.explanation: Since .NET Core, .NET is open source and cross-platform. Other languages run on it too, such as F# and Visual Basic, because they all compile to the same IL.
